v.t: Összegyűltek Mózes és Áron ellen, és azt mondták nekik: Túl sokat vállaltok! Az egész közösség szent, mindnyájan, és az Úr közöttük van. Miért emelkedtek hát az Úr gyülekezete fölé?

ve.t: They gathered against Moses and Aaron and said to them: You take too much on yourselves! The whole community is holy, all of them, and the LORD is among them. Why then do you set yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?

e.q: Amikor Mózes ezt meghallotta, ___.
e.qe: When Moses heard this, he ___.

v.t: Amikor Mózes ezt meghallotta, arcra esett.

ve.t: When Moses heard this, he fell on his face.

e.q: És most a ___ is keresitek?
e.qe: And now you are seeking the ___ as well?

v.t: Magához közelített téged és minden testvéredet, Lévi fiait veled; és most a papságot is keresitek?

ve.t: He brought you near, and all your brothers the sons of Levi with you; and now you are seeking the priesthood as well?

e.q: De azt mondták: ___!
e.qe: But they said: ___!

v.t: Mózes elküldött, hogy hívják Dátánt és Abirámot, Eliáb fiait. De azt mondták: Nem megyünk!

ve.t: Moses sent to call Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab. But they said: We will not come!

e.q: Egy ___ sem vettem el tőlük.
e.qe: I have not taken a single ___ from them.

v.t: Mózes nagyon megharagudott, és azt mondta az Úrnak: Ne tekints az ajándékukra! Egy szamarat sem vettem el tőlük, és egyiküknek sem tettem rosszat.

ve.t: Moses became very angry and said to the LORD: Do not look on their offering! I have not taken a single donkey from them, nor done wrong to any one of them.

e.q: ___ ezeknek az embereknek a sátraitól!
e.qe: ___ from the tents of these men!

v.t: Azt mondta a közösségnek: Távozzatok el ezeknek az embereknek a sátraitól, és semmihez ne érjetek, ami az övék.

ve.t: He said to the community: Move away from the tents of these men, and do not touch anything that belongs to them.

e.q: Ti öltétek meg az Úr ___!
e.qe: You have killed the people of the ___!

v.t: De másnap Izráel fiainak egész közössége zúgolódott Mózes és Áron ellen, és azt mondták: Ti öltétek meg az Úr népét!

ve.t: But the next day the whole community of the Israelites complained against Moses and Aaron and said: You have killed the people of the LORD!

e.q: Megállt a ___ és az élők között.
e.qe: He stood between the ___ and the living.

v.t: Megállt a halottak és az élők között, és megszűnt a csapás.

ve.t: He stood between the dead and the living, and the plague stopped.

m.q: Felkeltek Mózes ellen, és velük ___ ember.
m.qe: They rose up against Moses, and with them ___ men.

v.t: Felkeltek Mózes ellen, és velük kétszázötven ember Izráel fiai közül, a közösség vezetői, a gyülekezet választott, neves emberei.

ve.t: They rose up against Moses, and with them two hundred and fifty men of the Israelites, leaders of the community, chosen men of the assembly, men of name.

m.q: ___ megmutatja az Úr, ki az övé.
m.qe: ___ the LORD will show who is his.

v.t: Aztán azt mondta Kórahnak és az egész csoportjának: Reggel megmutatja az Úr, ki az övé, ki a szent, és akit magához közelít.

ve.t: Then he said to Korah and to all his group: In the morning the LORD will show who is his, who is holy, and whom he brings near to himself.

m.q: ___ nektek, hogy Izráel Istene kiválasztott titeket?
m.qe: Is it ___ for you that the God of Israel has chosen you?

v.t: Kevés nektek, hogy Izráel Istene kiválasztott titeket a közösségből, hogy magához közelítsen, hogy elvégezzétek az Úr hajlékának a szolgálatát?

ve.t: Is it too little for you that the God of Israel has chosen you out of the community to bring you near to himself, to carry out the service of the tabernacle of the LORD?

m.q: Ezért te és az egész csoportod az ___ ellen gyűltetek össze.
m.qe: So you and all your group have gathered against the ___.

v.t: Ezért te és az egész csoportod az Úr ellen gyűltetek össze. És Áron? Mi ő, hogy ellene zúgolódtok?

ve.t: So you and all your group have gathered against the LORD. And Aaron? What is he, that you complain against him?

m.q: Felhoztál minket arról a földről, amely ___ folyik.
m.qe: You brought us up from a land flowing with ___.

v.t: Kevés az, hogy felhoztál minket arról a földről, amely tejjel és mézzel folyik, hogy megölj minket a pusztában, és még uralkodni is akarsz rajtunk?

ve.t: Is it too little that you brought us up from a land flowing with milk and honey, to kill us in the wilderness, and now you want to rule over us as well?

m.q: Egy ember vétkezik, és te az egész ___ haragszol?
m.qe: One man sins, and will you be angry with the whole ___?

v.t: De ők arcra estek, és azt mondták: Isten, minden test lelkének az Istene! Egy ember vétkezik, és te az egész közösségre haragszol?

ve.t: But they fell on their faces and said: God, the God of the spirits of all flesh! One man sins, and will you be angry with the whole community?

m.q: Ebből tudjátok meg, hogy az Úr ___ engem.
m.qe: By this you will know that the LORD has ___ me.

v.t: Mózes azt mondta: Ebből tudjátok meg, hogy az Úr küldött engem, hogy mindezeket tegyem, és nem a magam szívéből.

ve.t: Moses said: By this you will know that the LORD has sent me to do all these things, and not from my own heart.

m.q: Áron fogta a ___, és odafutott a gyülekezet közé.
m.qe: Aaron took the ___ and ran into the middle of the assembly.

v.t: Áron fogta a füstölőt, ahogy Mózes mondta, és odafutott a gyülekezet közé; és íme, már elkezdődött a csapás a nép között. Betette a füstölőszert, és engesztelést szerzett a népért.

ve.t: Aaron took the censer, as Moses said, and ran into the middle of the assembly; and behold, the plague had already begun among the people. He put in the incense and made atonement for the people.

ve.t: They gathered against Moses and Aaron and said to them: You take too much on yourselves! The whole community is holy, all of them, and the LORD is among them. Why then do you set yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?

ve.t: Is it too little that you brought us up from a land flowing with milk and honey, to kill us in the wilderness, and now you want to rule over us as well?

v.t: De ha az Úr valami újat teremt, és megnyílik a föld, és elnyeli őket, akkor tudjátok meg, hogy ezek az emberek megvetették az Urat.

ve.t: But if the LORD creates something new, and the ground opens and swallows them, then you will know that these men have despised the LORD.

ve.t: Aaron took the censer, as Moses said, and ran into the middle of the assembly; and behold, the plague had already begun among the people. He put in the incense and made atonement for the people.

They said: you take too much on yourselves! The whole community is holy

m.q: Tedd sorrendbe a figyelmeztetést!
m.qe: Put the warning in order!

Mózes azt mondta a közösségnek: távozzatok el a sátraiktól

Moses said to the community: move away from their tents

By this you will know that the LORD has sent me

m.q: Tedd sorrendbe Mózes válaszát Kórahnak!
m.qe: Put the answer of Moses to Korah in order!
o: Amikor Mózes ezt meghallotta, arcra esett
Aztán azt mondta Kórahnak és az egész csoportjának
Reggel megmutatja az Úr, ki az övé és ki a szent
oe: When Moses heard this, he fell on his face
Then he said to Korah and to all his group
In the morning the LORD will show who is his and who is holy
And whom he brings near to himself

ve.t: Then he said to Korah and to all his group: In the morning the LORD will show who is his, who is holy, and whom he brings near to himself.

h.q: Tedd sorrendbe Korah ervének az elemzését!
h.qe: Put the analysis of the argument of Korah in order!
o: A 16:3-ban azt mondja: az egész kozosség szent, mindnyajan
Es ez az allitas IGAZ: a 2Moz 19:6 es a 3Moz 19:2 ugyanezt mondja
De a kovetkeztetés mas: ezert nekem is jar a papi hivatal
Vagyis egy igaz tanitasbol vont le olyat, ami nem kovetkezik belole
oe: In 16:3 he says: the whole community is holy, all of them
And this claim is TRUE: Ex 19:6 and Lev 19:2 say the same
But the conclusion is different: therefore the priestly office is mine too
So from a true teaching he drew what does not follow from it

v.t: Összegyűltek Mózes és Áron ellen, és azt mondták nekik: Túl sokat vállaltok! Az egész közösség szent, mindnyájan, és az Úr közöttük van. Miért emelkedtek hát az Úr gyülekezete fölé?

ve.t: They gathered against Moses and Aaron and said to them: You take too much on yourselves! The whole community is holy, all of them, and the LORD is among them. Why then do you set yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?

h.q: Tedd sorrendbe a ket szal kulonvalasztasat!
h.qe: Put the separating of the two strands in order!
o: A 16:1-11 Korahrol es a levitakrol szol: a kérdés a PAPSAG
A 16:12-15 Datanrol es Abiramrol szol: a kérdés a VEZETES
A ket csoport mas vadat emel, es mas a sorsuk is
Sok kutato ket eredetileg kulon elbeszelest lat benne - de ezt nem tudjuk biztosan
oe: 16:1-11 is about Korah and the Levites: the question is the PRIESTHOOD
16:12-15 is about Dathan and Abiram: the question is LEADERSHIP
The two groups bring different charges and have different fates
Many scholars see two originally separate accounts - but we do not know for certain

v.t: Mózes elküldött, hogy hívják Dátánt és Abirámot, Eliáb fiait. De azt mondták: Nem megyünk!

ve.t: Moses sent to call Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab. But they said: We will not come!

h.q: Tedd sorrendbe Korah fiainak a sorsat!
h.qe: Put the fate of the sons of Korah in order!
o: A 16:32 szerint a fold elnyelte oket es a hazaikat
De a 4Mozes 26:11 kifejezetten azt mondja: Korah fiai nem haltak meg
A Korahitak kesobb a templomi enekesek lettek
Tizenegy zsoltar all Korah fiainak a nevével (Zsolt 42; 44-49; 84-85; 87-88)
oe: By 16:32 the ground swallowed them and their households
But Numbers 26:11 expressly says: the sons of Korah did not die
The Korahites later became the temple singers
Eleven psalms stand with the name of the sons of Korah (Ps 42; 44-49; 84-85; 87-88)

v.t: De ha az Úr valami újat teremt, és megnyílik a föld, és elnyeli őket, akkor tudjátok meg, hogy ezek az emberek megvetették az Urat.

ve.t: But if the LORD creates something new, and the ground opens and swallows them, then you will know that these men have despised the LORD.

story.e:
**A Sentence That Was True — and Still Led to Trouble**

This is the hardest chapter in Numbers. Many people die in it, and we will not say that it is easy reading.

But there is something in it that is very interesting and worth noticing.

**Who Were They?**

**Korah** was a Levite (16:1) — from the same tribe as Moses and Aaron. The Levites were the ones who carried out the service of the holy tent.

**Dathan and Abiram** were from the sons of Reuben. They were not speaking about the service but about who leads the people.

And with them **two hundred and fifty men** — and notice what the text says about them (16:2): *leaders of the community, chosen men of the assembly, **men of name.***

So it was not the ignorant who rebelled. It was the important men.

**And Now the Sentence to Notice**

*You take too much on yourselves! **The whole community is holy, all of them,** and the LORD is among them. Why then do you set yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?* (16:3)

Read the middle: *the whole community is holy, all of them.*

**This is true.**

In Exodus 19:6 God himself said: *you will be a holy nation.* And in Leviticus 19:2 (we read this in p43): *be holy, because I am holy.*

So Korah spoke a **true teaching.**

**Then What Was the Trouble?**

That what he **drew from it** did not follow from it.

Moses answers this (16:9-10):

*Is it too little for you that the God of Israel has chosen you... to carry out the service of the tabernacle of the LORD? He brought you near, and all your brothers with you... and now **you are seeking the priesthood as well?***

That is: you have already received something — and now you want the other thing too.

And it is worth comparing with something. Do you remember p47? There **Moses** said (11:29): *if only **all** the people of the LORD were prophets!*

Moses wanted **everyone to receive.** Korah wanted **himself** to get the office.

The same words — a different intent.

**Dathan and Abiram Spoke About Something Else**

Moses called them, but they answered (16:12): ***We will not come!***

And their argument (16:13): *Is it too little that you brought us up from a land **flowing with milk and honey,** to kill us in the wilderness?*

Now notice. Which land are they talking about?

**Egypt.**

So the phrase — *a land flowing with milk and honey* — which the Bible always uses for the **promised land,** they now apply to **Egypt.**

**The Answer of Moses**

Moses became angry and said this (16:15):

*Do not look on their offering! **I have not taken a single donkey from them,** nor done wrong to any one of them.*

That is: *account with me. I never took anything from you.*

That is the answer of an honest leader. (And here is something interesting: many years later **Samuel** says almost exactly the same — 1 Sam 12:3.)

**And Now Something Worth Noticing**

God says he will make an end of the community. And Moses and Aaron **fall on their faces** and say (16:22):

*God, the God of the spirits of all flesh! **One man sins, and will you be angry with the whole community?***

Moses and Aaron spoke for those who had stood against them. Again.

And the answer was that the community had to be **separated** (16:24-26). So their question received an answer.

**The Hard Part**

The ground opened and swallowed Korah, Dathan, Abiram and their households. And fire came out and consumed the two hundred and fifty men.

This is terrible, and we will not soften it. Anyone who reads it and is horrified read it rightly.

But there is something the Bible itself adds, which must not be left out.

**Numbers 26:11:** *But the sons of Korah **did not die.***

So the descendants of Korah did not perish.

**And Do You Know What Became of Them?**

**Temple singers.**

Look at the book of Psalms. Above eleven psalms stands this: *of the sons of Korah.* Psalms 42; 44-49; 84-85; 87-88.

So the descendants of the man who wanted to seize the priestly office ended up **singing** in the temple. They did not receive it the way he wanted — but another way.

**And the Loveliest Part of the Chapter**

The next day the people complained again — now about what had happened (16:41): *You have killed the people of the LORD!*

And a plague came among the people. And then this happened (16:47-48):

*Aaron took the **censer,** as Moses said, and **ran into the middle of the assembly...** He put in the incense and made atonement for the people. **He stood between the dead and the living,** and the plague stopped.*

Notice two things.

**One:** Aaron **ran towards** those who a day earlier had called him a murderer.

**Two:** and he did it **with the censer.** Precisely the object the whole rebellion had been about — the right to bring incense before God.

The same object that was the cause of the dispute became the thing with which he saved the people.

**What Comes Next?**

In p52 comes Numbers 17: **the budding staff of Aaron.** Twelve staffs are laid down in the tent, and the next morning one of them has blossoms and fruit. And this will be the answer to the question Korah asked.
story.m:
**A Sentence That Was True — and Still Led to Trouble**

This is the hardest chapter in Numbers. More people die in it than in any other chapter of the book, and we will not soften that.

But the chapter is not only about that. It contains a very precise observation about how a **true sentence** becomes a false conclusion.

**Two (or Three) Groups — and Two Different Questions**

It is worth separating the characters, because they did **not want the same thing:**

| Who | From where | What they wanted |
|---|---|---|
| **Korah** | from the tribe of Levi (16:1) | the **priesthood** (16:10) |
| **Dathan and Abiram** | from the sons of Reuben (16:1) | the **leadership** (16:13) |
| **the two hundred and fifty** | leaders of the community (16:2) | to bring incense (16:17) |

So in this chapter **two different disputes** run side by side:

- **the question of priesthood:** who may bring incense before God?
- **the question of leadership:** who says where we go?

This is worth seeing, because the two groups bring different charges and their fates differ too.

And one more thing: by 16:2 the two hundred and fifty men are *leaders of the community, chosen men of the assembly, **men of name.*** So it was not the ignorant who rebelled but the most important men.

**And Now the Sentence That Is the Key to the Chapter**

*You take too much on yourselves! **The whole community is holy, all of them,** and the LORD is among them. Why then do you set yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?* (16:3)

At first this sentence sounds like rebellion. But read the middle once more:

*The whole community is holy, all of them.*

**This is true.** And Korah did not invent it:

| Place | What it says |
|---|---|
| Ex 19:6 | *you will be a holy nation* |
| Lev 19:2 (p43) | *be holy, because I, the LORD, am holy* |
| Deut 7:6 | *you are a holy people to the LORD your God* |

So Korah quoted a **teaching** that God had given to the people.

**Then What Was the Trouble?**

That the **conclusion** did not follow from it.

From *the whole people is holy* it does not follow that *therefore everyone may carry out every service.* These are two different things: **belonging** and **task.**

And the answer of Moses goes to exactly this (16:9-10):

*Is it too little for you that the God of Israel has chosen you out of the community to bring you near to himself, to carry out the service of the tabernacle of the LORD? He brought you near, and all your brothers the sons of Levi with you; and now **you are seeking the priesthood as well?***

There are two things in this answer:

1. **You have already received something.** The service of the Levites was no small thing.
2. **And now you want the other thing too.**

**And an Important Comparison**

Do you remember p47? There Moses said (11:29): *If only **all** the people of the LORD were prophets, and the LORD would put his spirit on them!*

Now compare the two:

| | Moses (11:29) | Korah (16:3) |
|---|---|---|
| What he says | if only everyone received | the whole people is holy, all of them |
| What he wants | that **others** receive | that **he** gets the office |
| For whom he speaks | for the others | for himself |

Almost the same words — and an entirely different intent. This is the finest observation in the chapter.

**Dathan and Abiram — Another Dispute**

Moses sent for them, but they answered (16:12): ***We will not come!***

Refusing the conversation was also a decision.

And their argument (16:13-14):

*Is it too little that you brought us up from a land **flowing with milk and honey,** to kill us in the wilderness, and now you want to rule over us as well? You have not brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey either, nor given us fields and vineyards as an inheritance.*

Two things are worth noticing here.

**One: the swap.** The phrase *a land flowing with milk and honey* in the Bible **always** means the promised land (Ex 3:8; Lev 20:24; Num 13:27). And Dathan and Abiram now use it for **Egypt.**

So they do not only leave something out — they **swap** the two lands.

**Two: what they leave out.** It is true that they did not get into the land. But the **why** is in chapter 14 (p50): their own decision. That they do not mention.

**The Answer of Moses — and an Honest Accounting**

*Moses became very angry and said to the LORD: Do not look on their offering! **I have not taken a single donkey from them,** nor done wrong to any one of them.* (16:15)

This is the answer of a leader who can account for what he received from his service.

And here is something interesting: **Samuel,** many years later, when handing over the leadership, says almost exactly the same (1 Sam 12:3): *whose donkey have I taken? Whom have I oppressed?*

**And Now What Is Worth Noticing: Moses Intercedes Again**

God says he will make an end of the community (16:21). And then Moses and Aaron **fall on their faces** (16:22):

*God, the God of the spirits of all flesh! **One man sins, and will you be angry with the whole community?***

There are three things in this:

1. **For whom do they speak?** For the people who had just gathered against them. Just as in p50.
2. **What do they argue with?** A question that is a real objection: it is not right that the many should bear the act of one man.
3. **And what is the answer?** In 16:23-26 God says that the community must be **separated.** So their objection was **accepted.**

**The Hard Part**

By 16:28-33 the ground opened and swallowed Korah, Dathan, Abiram and their households. Then fire came out and consumed the two hundred and fifty men.

This is terrible, and we will not call it anything else. And by 16:27 their families were standing there too.

We add two things, and both come from the Bible.

**The first (Numbers 26:11):** *But the sons of Korah **did not die.***

The Bible itself clarifies. The whole line did not perish.

**The second:** and do you know what became of the descendants of Korah?

**Temple singers.**

Look at the book of Psalms:

| Psalms | With whose name |
|---|---|
| 42; 44-49 | *of the sons of Korah* |
| 84-85; 87-88 | *of the sons of Korah* |

Eleven psalms. And by 1 Chronicles 9:19 and 26:1 the Korahites were the **gatekeepers** and singers of the temple.

So the descendants of the man who wanted the holy service by force ended up **in** the service — but not in the way he wanted.

**And the Loveliest Part of the Chapter**

The next day the people complained again — now about what had happened (16:41): *You have killed the people of the LORD!*

So the great event did **not** change them.

And a plague came among them. And then this happened (16:47-48):

*Aaron took the **censer,** as Moses said, and **ran into the middle of the assembly;** and behold, the plague had already begun. He put in the incense and made atonement for the people. **He stood between the dead and the living,** and the plague stopped.*

Notice three things:

**One: the direction of the running.** Aaron ran **towards** where the plague was — among those who a day earlier had called him a murderer.

**Two: the object.** Aaron did it **with the censer.** Precisely the object the whole rebellion had been about: the right to bring incense before God.

The same object that was the cause of the dispute became the thing with which he saved the people.

**Three: the place.** *He stood between the dead and the living.* This is the last image of the chapter — and it is the clearest description of priestly service in the whole five books of Moses.

**What Comes Next?**

In p52 comes Numbers 17: **the budding staff of Aaron.**

Twelve staffs are laid down in the tent — one from each tribe. And the next morning one of them has blossoms and **almonds** on it.

And this will be the answer to the question Korah asked: not by a vote, not by force, but by something beginning to live.
story.h:
**A Sentence That Was True — and Still Led to Trouble**

This is the hardest chapter in Numbers. Let us say it at the outset: more people die in it than in any other chapter of the book, and we will not soften that. Nor will we dwell in it.

But there are four things in the chapter worth thinking through precisely:

1. that the sentence of Korah was **true**
2. that **two** different disputes run side by side in this chapter
3. that Dathan and Abiram **swap** a biblical phrase
4. and what the Bible itself adds about the descendants of Korah

**1. The Two (or Three) Strands**

It is worth separating the characters of chapter 16, because they did **not want the same thing:**

| Who | From where | Their question | Where in the text |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Korah** | Levi, the clan of Kohath | the **priesthood** | 16:1-11, 16-24, 35 |
| **Dathan and Abiram** | Reuben | the **leadership** | 16:12-15, 25-34 |
| **the two hundred and fifty** | leaders of the community | to bring incense | 16:2, 16-18, 35 |

The two main strands are distinct both **grammatically and in content:**

| | The strand of Korah | The strand of Dathan and Abiram |
|---|---|---|
| The charge | *why do you set yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?* (16:3) | *you want to rule over us* (16:13) |
| Addressed to | Moses **and Aaron** | Moses **only** |
| The subject | holiness and priesthood | leadership and land |
| The test | censers (16:16-18) | none |

Many scholars conclude from this that the chapter is the weaving together of two originally **separate** accounts. That is **possible,** but we do not know for certain — and the text stands before us in its present form as one chapter.

What we can say for certain: the two strands are **clearly separable,** and it is worth reading them separately, because they ask different questions.

**And a Note About the Two Hundred and Fifty**

16:2 names them precisely: *leaders of the community, chosen men of the assembly, **men of name*** (in Hebrew *keruei moed, anshei shem*).

So it was **not** the ignorant who rebelled. It was the most respected men.

**2. 16:3 — the Sentence That Is True**

*You take too much on yourselves! **The whole community is holy, all of them,** and the LORD is among them. Why then do you set yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?*

This is the most important point of the chapter, and it is worth going through slowly.

**Is it true that the whole community is holy?**

Yes. And Korah was not the first to state it:

| Place | What it says |
|---|---|
| Ex 19:6 | *a priestly kingdom and a **holy nation** you will be* |
| Lev 19:2 (p43) | *be holy, because I, the LORD your God, am holy* |
| Deut 7:6 | *you are a **holy people** to the LORD your God* |
| Deut 14:2 | the same |

So Korah quoted back one of the **basic teachings of the covenant.**

**Then where is the error?**

In the **conclusion.** Let us see what follows and what does not:

| The claim | What follows from it |
|---|---|
| the whole people is holy (belonging) | that the whole people belongs to God — **true** |
| therefore everyone may carry out every service | **does not follow** |

In the language of Exodus and Leviticus holiness means: **set apart, belonging to God** (we discussed this in detail in p43). That is about **belonging,** not about **tasks.**

And the answer of Moses points to exactly this difference (16:9-10):

*Is it too little for you that the God of Israel has chosen you out of the community to **bring you near to himself,** to carry out the service of the tabernacle of the LORD? He brought you near, and all your brothers the sons of Levi with you; and now **you are seeking the priesthood as well?***

Notice the phrase that occurs twice: *brought near.* The Levites **already** had the nearness. The question was not belonging but office.

**And Now the Finest Observation in This Part**

Compare the sentence of Korah with the sentence of Moses from p47:

| | Moses (Num 11:29) | Korah (Num 16:3) |
|---|---|---|
| The sentence | *if only **all** the people of the LORD were prophets* | *the whole community is holy, **all of them*** |
| The subject | the giving of the spirit | holiness |
| For whom he speaks | **for others** | **for himself** |
| What he asks | that others receive too | that he receive the office too |
| His own position | he already has it | he already has it |

The two sentences claim almost the same thing. The **intent** is different.

And this is not our interpretation: in 16:10 Moses states what he sees in it (*you are seeking the priesthood as well*), and in 16:11 he names what it really is: *you and all your group have gathered **against the LORD.***

**3. Dathan and Abiram — and a Swap**

Moses sent for them (16:12), and their answer: ***we will not come!***

Refusing the conversation is itself a decision. And their argument (16:13-14):

*Is it too little that you brought us up from a land **flowing with milk and honey,** to kill us in the wilderness, and now you want to rule over us as well? You have not brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey either, nor given us fields and vineyards as an inheritance.*

Two things are worth examining.

**The first: the swapping of the phrase.**

*A land flowing with milk and honey* (in Hebrew *erets zavat halav u-dvash*) in the Bible **always** means the promised land:

| Place | What it refers to |
|---|---|
| Ex 3:8, 17 | Canaan |
| Lev 20:24 | Canaan |
| Num 13:27 (p49) | Canaan — the scouts called it this too |
| Deut 6:3; 11:9 | Canaan |

And Dathan and Abiram now use it for **Egypt.**

This is not simple nostalgia (as the fish and the onions in p47). This is a **swap:** they turn the phrase that points forward into one that points back.

So by 16:13 the promised land is no longer Canaan but Egypt. Anger rewrote the meaning of the words too.

**The second: what they leave out.**

The first half of 16:14 is **true:** he really did not bring them into the land.

But the **why** is in chapter 14 (p50): they themselves decided not to go up. And when they went the next day, by 14:44-45 they were defeated.

So the charge names a true fact but **leaves out their own part** in it.

**4. The Accounting of Moses — and a Parallel**

*Moses became very angry and said to the LORD: Do not look on their offering! **I have not taken a single donkey from them,** nor done wrong to any one of them.* (16:15)

This is a public **financial accounting.** Moses does not say that he is a good man. He says that nothing in his possession can be traced to the people.

And here is a lovely biblical parallel. **Samuel,** many years later, when he hands over the leadership, says almost exactly the same (1 Sam 12:3):

*Whose ox have I taken? Whose **donkey** have I taken? Whom have I oppressed?*

So the Bible twice describes with the same sentence how an honest leader accounts for himself.

**5. 16:22 — and an Objection God Accepts**

God tells Moses and Aaron to stand away from the community, because he will make an end of them (16:21).

And then this happens (16:22):

*But they **fell on their faces** and said: God, the God of the spirits of all flesh! **One man sins, and will you be angry with the whole community?***

Three things are worth seeing here.

**One: for whom they speak.** For the people who had gathered **against them.** This is the second such intercession within two chapters (cf. 14:13-19, p50).

**Two: what they argue with.** They do not say that the people are good. They make a **point of principle:** it is not right that the many should bear the act of one man.

This question runs through the Bible:

| Place | What it says |
|---|---|
| Gen 18:23-25 | Abraham: *would you destroy the righteous with the wicked?* |
| Num 16:22 | *one man sins, and will you be angry with the whole community?* |
| Ezek 18:2-4 | *you will not die for the offence of the fathers* |
| Jer 31:29-30 | the same |

**Three, and this matters most: the answer.** In 16:23-26 God says that the community must **move away** from the tents of the rebels.

So their question **received an answer,** and the objection was **not disregarded.** The separating of the community is exactly what they asked for.

**6. The Hard Part — Which We Do Not Omit and Do Not Dwell In**

By 16:28-35:

- the ground opened and swallowed Korah, Dathan, Abiram and their households (16:31-33)
- fire came out and consumed the **two hundred and fifty** men (16:35)

We say four things about this.

**One.** This is terrible, and we will not call it anything else. By 16:27 the families were standing there at the entrances of the tents. Anyone who reads this and is horrified **read it rightly.**

**Two.** The text itself calls what happened **unusual.** The phrase of 16:30: *if the LORD **creates something new*** (in Hebrew *im beriah yivra* — if he creates a creation). So the text does not speak of it as an ordinary event.

**Three.** In 16:28-30 Moses says **in advance** what the sign will be. He does not explain it afterwards but states beforehand what to watch for.

**Four, and the Bible itself adds this:** **Numbers 26:11** says: ***But the sons of Korah did not die.***

This is not our softening. It is the clarification of the Bible: the whole line did not perish.

**7. And Now the Loveliest Thing in This Chapter: What Became of the Descendants of Korah**

This is one of the most important contents of p51, because almost no one knows it.

The descendants of Korah, the **Korahites,** became the **singers** of the temple service.

| Where | What it says |
|---|---|
| 1 Chron 6:22-28 | the genealogy of the Korahites, including **Samuel** |
| 1 Chron 9:19 | the Korahites were the **gatekeepers** of the tent |
| 1 Chron 26:1, 19 | the Korahites as gatekeepers of the temple |
| 2 Chron 20:19 | the Korahites praised God **in song** |
| Ps 42; 44-49; 84-85; 87-88 | **eleven psalms** with their name: *of the sons of Korah* |

Read Psalm 84. It is a psalm of the sons of Korah, and this is its first line: *How lovely are your dwellings, LORD of hosts!*

And 84:10: *I would rather be a **doorkeeper** in the house of my God than live in the tents of the wicked.*

Now read it again and think through **whose** descendants wrote this.

Korah wanted the priestly office by force. His descendants wrote that it is better to be a **doorkeeper.**

This is one of the loveliest, quietest turns in the Bible. And it is not our invention: the headings of the psalms are there in the text.

**8. The Next Day — and the Running of Aaron**

The opening of 16:41 is painful: *but **the next day** the whole community of the Israelites complained against Moses and Aaron and said: **You have killed the people of the LORD!***

So the great event did **not** change them. One day later they were already accusing Moses and Aaron.

And a plague came among them. And then this happened (16:47-48):

*Aaron took the **censer,** as Moses said, and **ran into the middle of the assembly;** and behold, the plague had already begun among the people. He put in the incense and made atonement for the people. **He stood between the dead and the living,** and the plague stopped.*

Three observations.

**The first: the direction of the running.** The Hebrew *wayyarots* — *and he ran.* Aaron ran **towards** where the plague was. Among those who a day earlier had called him a murderer.

**The second: the object.** Aaron stopped the plague **with the censer.**

And now think through what the rebellion had been about. By 16:6-7 and 16:17-18 the test was precisely about **the censers:** who may bring incense before God.

So **the same object** that the dispute was about became the thing with which Aaron saved those who had started the dispute.

And by 16:38-39 the censers of the rebels were hammered into plates and overlaid on the altar — as a reminder. So the object they had demanded ended up hammered onto the altar.

**The third: the place.** *He stood between the dead and the living.*

This is the last image of the chapter. And it is perhaps the clearest description of what priestly service means in the whole five books of Moses: **standing in the hardest place.**

**9. What Does the New Testament Say About This?**

**Jude 11** mentions it briefly: *they perished in the rebellion of Korah.*

And it is worth noting what the letter warns against: the arbitrary seizing of authority, not the asking of the question.

For the Bible itself asks the question. **1 Peter 2:9** writes of believers: *a chosen people, a **royal priesthood,** a holy nation* — and that is precisely the language of Exodus 19:6, which Korah also quoted.

So the question Korah asked was **not a forbidden question.** The New Testament itself gives an answer to it — only not in the way Korah wanted.

**What Comes Next?**

In p52 comes Numbers 17: **the budding staff of Aaron.**

Twelve staffs are laid down in the tent, one from each tribe, with the name written on it. And the next morning **one** of them has blossoms and ripe **almonds.**

And this is the answer to the question of Korah: not by a vote, not by force, not even by argument — but by something **beginning to live** on a dead branch of wood.

verse.text: He stood between the dead and the living, and the plague stopped.

story.e:
**Tizenkét holt faág — és másnap reggel az egyiken mandula van**

A p51-ben Kórah feltett egy kérdést: ki vihet füstölőszert Isten elé? Ki lehet pap?

És most jön a válasz. De nem úgy, ahogy várnád.

**Nem szavazás. Nem erőpróba. Nem vita.**

Így szólt a próba (17:2):

*Vegyél tőlük egy-egy botot minden nemzetség szerint, az atyáik házának minden vezetőjétől, **tizenkét botot;** mindegyiknek a nevét írd rá a botjára.*

Tizenkét **bot.** Mindegyikre rá volt írva, kié.

És most figyelj valamire, ami fontos.

**Mi az a bot?**

A bot egy **levágott faág.** Valaki valamikor levágta egy fáról, lefaragta, és azóta használja — támaszkodik rá, hajtja vele a nyájat.

Vagyis a bot **holt fa.** Nincs gyökere, nincs levele, nem nő, és nem virágzik.

És ez a próba lényege.

**Mit mondott Isten?**

*Annak az embernek a botja, akit kiválasztok, **kivirágzik.*** (17:5)

Nem azt mondta: aki a legerősebb. Nem azt: aki a legokosabb. Nem azt: akire a legtöbben szavaznak.

Azt mondta: amelyik bot **élni kezd.**

**Mi történt?**

Mózes letette mind a tizenkét botot a sátorban, Isten elé (17:7). Áron botja is **a többi között** volt (17:6) — nem kapott külön helyet.

És másnap (17:8):

*Másnap Mózes bement a bizonyság sátorába, és íme, **Áron botja** kivirágzott: **bimbót hajtott, virágot nyitott, és mandulát termett.***

Olvasd el a végét még egyszer, és számold meg, hány dolog van benne:

1. **bimbót hajtott**
2. **virágot nyitott**
3. **mandulát termett**

Három szakasz — és **mind a három egyszerre** van ott a boton.

A valóságban ez hónapokat venne igénybe: először bimbó, aztán virág, aztán — sokkal később — a beért gyümölcs. Itt mind a három ott van egyszerre.

**Miért éppen mandula?**

Ez szép részlet. A **mandulafa** az első fa, amely kinyílik azon a földön — januárban vagy februárban, amikor még minden más alszik.

Vagyis a mandula a **legkorábbi ébredés** jele.

**És mi történt utána?**

*Mózes kivitte az összes botot az Úr elől Izráel minden fiához; és **látták,** és mindegyik elvette a maga botját.* (17:9)

Mindenki látta. Nem titkos jel volt.

És Isten azt mondta, hogy Áron botját **tegyék vissza** a bizonyság elé, *hogy megőrizzék **jelül*** (17:10). Vagyis később is meg lehessen nézni.

**És most jön valami, amire nem számítanál**

Azt gondolnád, hogy a nép megnyugodott. Hiszen megvan a válasz.

De nem ez történt (17:12-13):

*Izráel fiai azt mondták Mózesnek: Íme, **elpusztulunk, elvesztünk, mindnyájan elvesztünk!** Mindenki, aki az Úr hajlékához közelít, meghal. Vajon egészen el kell pusztulnunk?*

Vagyis nem megnyugodtak. **Megrémültek.**

A kérdés el volt döntve — és ettől még jobban féltek.

**És mit válaszolt Isten erre?**

Ez a legérdekesebb része az egésznek.

Isten **nem** azt mondta, hogy *ne félj, nincs semmi baj.* Hanem ezt (18:1):

*Te és a fiaid és atyád háza veled együtt **hordozzátok a szentély bűnét;** te és a fiaid hordozzátok a papságotok bűnét.*

Vagyis: a félelem jogos — de nem nektek kell hordoznotok. **A papok hordozzák.**

És a 18:5 megmondja, miért: *hogy **ne legyen többé harag** Izráel fiain.*

Vagyis a papi szolgálat nem azért volt, hogy valaki fontos legyen. Azért volt, hogy a nép **biztonságban** legyen.

**És a legszebb mondat**

*Te pedig és a fiaid veled együtt végezzétek a papságot... **Ajándékul adtam nektek a papságotokat.*** (18:7)

**Ajándékul.**

Most gondold végig, mi volt Kórah kérdése: *miért nem lehet az enyém is?*

És a válasz: mert ez nem olyan dolog, amit **meg lehet szerezni.** Ez olyan dolog, amit **adnak.**

**Mi lesz a következő részben?**

A p53-ban jön a 4Mózes 20: **víz a sziklából** — és ez lesz az a nap, amikor Mózes hibázik. És abban a fejezetben hal meg Mirjám és Áron is.

Ez a 4Mózes egyik legszomorúbb fejezete.
story.m:
**Tizenkét holt faág — és másnap reggel az egyiken mandula van**

A p51-ben Kórah feltett egy kérdést: **ki lehet pap?** Ki vihet füstölőszert Isten elé?

És most jön a válasz. De a válasz módja a legérdekesebb benne.

**Mi NEM volt a próba**

Érdemes először azt látni, mit **nem** tett Isten:

| Amit nem tett | Pedig lehetett volna |
|---|---|
| nem szavaztatta meg a népet | hiszen a 16:3 szerint az egész nép szent |
| nem rendezett erőpróbát | hiszen a füstölők próbája már megvolt (16:16-18) |
| nem vitatkozott | hiszen Mózes már érvelt (16:9-11) |
| nem Mózesre bízta a döntést | hiszen ő volt a vezető |

Hanem ezt tette (17:2):

*Vegyél tőlük egy-egy botot minden nemzetség szerint... **tizenkét botot;** mindegyiknek a nevét írd rá a botjára.*

**Mi az a bot?**

Ezen érdemes megállni, mert ez a próba kulcsa.

A bot egy **levágott faág.** Lefaragott, kiszárított fa. Nincs gyökere, nincs levele, nem vesz fel vizet, és nem növekszik.

Vagyis a bot pontosan az a dolog, amely **nem tud kivirágozni.**

És Isten éppen ezzel próbál (17:5):

*Annak az embernek a botja, akit kiválasztok, **kivirágzik;** így elhallgattatom előlem Izráel fiainak a zúgolódását.*

Figyeld meg, mi a jel: nem az erő, nem a szám, nem a vita. Hanem az, hogy valami **élni kezd** ott, ahol nem lehet élet.

**A lebonyolítás — és egy fontos részlet**

| Vers | Mi történik |
|---|---|
| 17:2-3 | tizenkét bot, mindegyiken a vezető nevével; Áron neve Lévi botjára |
| 17:6 | mindegyik vezető ad egy botot — és **Áron botja is közöttük van** |
| 17:7 | Mózes leteszi mindet az Úr elé |
| 17:8 | **másnap** Áron botja kivirágzott |
| 17:9 | Mózes kivitte mindet, és **mindenki látta** |
| 17:10 | Áron botját vissza kell tenni, **jelül** |

Két részletet érdemes megjegyezni.

**Az első:** a 17:6 szerint *Áron botja is **közöttük** volt.* Vagyis nem kapott külön helyet. Ugyanúgy letették, mint a többit.

**A második:** a 17:9 szerint Mózes **kivitte** a botokat, és a nép *látta.* A jel nyilvános volt — nem Mózes jelentette be, hanem mindenki a saját szemével látta.

**A 17:8 — három szakasz egyszerre**

*És íme, Áron botja, Lévi háza botja kivirágzott: **bimbót hajtott, virágot nyitott, és mandulát termett.***

Számold meg, hány dolog van ebben a félmondatban:

| Szakasz | Normálisan mikor |
|---|---|
| bimbó | a virágzás előtt |
| virág | tavasszal, pár napig |
| beért mandula | **hónapokkal** később |

A három szakasz a valóságban nem fordulhat elő **egyszerre** egy ágon. A szöveg szándékosan halmozza őket.

**Miért éppen mandula?**

Ez nem véletlen választás, és érdemes tudni, miért.

A **mandulafa** az első fa, amely kinyílik azon a földön: januárban vagy februárban, amikor minden más még alszik. Héberül *sáked.*

És ebből lesz egy szójáték a Bibliában. A **Jeremiás 1:11-12**-ben Isten egy **mandulavesszőt** mutat a prófétának, és azt mondja: *jól láttál, mert **virrasztok** a szavam fölött, hogy beteljesítsem.* A *virraszt* szó héberül *sókéd* — szinte ugyanúgy hangzik, mint a *sáked* (mandula).

Vagyis a mandula a Bibliában az **éberség** és a **korai ébredés** jele.

És még valami: a **menóra,** a szent sátor lámpatartója, mandulavirág alakú kelyhekkel volt díszítve (2Móz 25:33-34).

**És most jön valami, amire nem számítanál**

Azt gondolnád, hogy a nép megnyugszik. Megvan a válasz, a jel nyilvános volt, mindenki látta.

De ez történt (17:12-13):

*Izráel fiai azt mondták Mózesnek: Íme, **elpusztulunk, elvesztünk, mindnyájan elvesztünk!** Mindenki, aki az Úr hajlékához közelít, meghal. Vajon egészen el kell pusztulnunk?*

Vagyis **nem megnyugodtak. Megrémültek.**

A kérdés el volt döntve — és a félelmük ettől nem lett kevesebb, hanem több. Most azt látták, hogy a szentély **közelsége veszélyes.**

Ez emberileg pontos megfigyelés: a bizonyíték és a bizalom nem ugyanaz.

**És Isten válasza — ami a legérdekesebb**

A 18. fejezet első versei **pontosan erre a kérdésre** válaszolnak. És nézd meg, hogyan.

Isten **nem** azt mondja, hogy *ne félj, nincs veszély.* Ezt mondja (18:1):

*Te és a fiaid és atyád háza veled együtt **hordozzátok a szentély bűnét;** te és a fiaid hordozzátok a papságotok bűnét.*

Vagyis: a félelem **nem alaptalan** — de a terhet valaki hordozza. És nem a nép.

És a 18:5 megadja a célt: *hogy **ne legyen többé harag** Izráel fiain.*

Ez az egész papi szolgálat értelme ebben a fejezetben. Nem a rang. Nem a kiváltság. **A teher.**

**És most a legszebb mondat**

*Te pedig és a fiaid veled együtt végezzétek a papságot mindabban, ami az oltárhoz és a függöny mögé tartozik. **Ajándékul adtam nektek a papságotokat.*** (18:7)

Az *ajándékul* szó héberül *mattáná* — ajándék.

És most vesd össze ezt Kórah kérésével:

| Kórah (16:10) | A válasz (18:7) |
|---|---|
| *a papságot is keresitek* | *ajándékul adtam nektek* |
| meg akarta szerezni | olyan dolog, amelyet csak **adni** lehet |

Vagyis a válasz nem az, hogy Kórah rossz volt és Áron jó. A válasz az, hogy **ez nem olyan dolog, amit meg lehet szerezni.**

És érdemes megjegyezni: a 18:6 szerint a **léviták** is *ajándékul adattak* a papoknak. Vagyis mind a kettő ajándék volt. Senki nem érdemelte ki.

**Mi lesz a következő részben?**

A p53-ban jön a 4Mózes 20: **víz a sziklából.**

Ez a 4Mózes egyik legszomorúbb fejezete. Három dolog történik benne:

- meghal **Mirjám** (20:1), egyetlen rövid mondatban
- **Mózes hibázik** a szikla előtt (20:10-12)
- és meghal **Áron** (20:28)

És ott lesz a kérdés, amelyet nem lehet kihagyni: mit tett Mózes olyan rosszul, hogy nem mehetett be a földre?
story.h:
**Tizenkét holt faág — és másnap reggel az egyiken mandula van**

A p51-ben Kórah feltett egy kérdést, és a kérdés jó volt: **ki lehet pap?** Ki vihet füstölőszert Isten elé?

Ez a rész a választ tartalmazza. És a válasz módja a legérdekesebb benne.

Négy dologgal lesz dolgunk:

1. a próba **természete** — és miért éppen bottal
2. a 17:8 **három szakasza** egyszerre
3. a mandula, és egy szójáték Jeremiásnál
4. és a legfontosabb: hogy a nép reakciója **nem** megnyugvás volt — és mit válaszolt erre Isten

**Egy megjegyzés a számozásról**

Mielőtt belekezdünk, egy gyakorlati dolog, amely zavaró lehet.

A **héber** Bibliában ezek a versek a **17:16-28** számot kapják. Ez azért van, mert a héber szöveg a 17. fejezetet ott kezdi, ahol a magyar és az angol Bibliák többsége a 16. fejezet végét teszi (a füstölők lemezei és a csapás).

Vagyis:

| Mi | Magyar és angol számozás | Héber számozás |
|---|---|---|
| a füstölők lemezei | 16:36-40 | 17:1-5 |
| a csapás és Áron futása | 16:41-50 | 17:6-15 |
| **a tizenkét bot** | **17:1-13** | **17:16-28** |

Mi a magyar Bibliákban megszokott számozást követjük, ahogy a játék többi részében is. De ha valaki más Bibliában keresi, lehet, hogy más számokat talál. Ez nem hiba, hanem két hagyomány.

**1. A próba természete — és miért éppen bottal**

Először azt érdemes látni, mit **nem** tett Isten:

| Amit nem tett | Pedig logikus lett volna |
|---|---|
| nem szavaztatott | a 16:3 szerint az egész nép szent — kézenfekvő lett volna megkérdezni |
| nem rendezett erőpróbát | a füstölők próbája ilyen volt (16:16-18) |
| nem vitatkozott tovább | Mózes már érvelt (16:9-11) |
| nem Mózes döntött | holott ő volt a vezető |

Hanem ezt rendelte (17:2):

*Vegyél tőlük egy-egy botot minden nemzetség szerint, az atyáik házának minden vezetőjétől, **tizenkét botot;** mindegyiknek a nevét írd rá a botjára.*

**Most gondold végig, mi egy bot.**

A héber szó: *matte.* Jelentése bot, vessző, pálca — és ugyanez a szó jelenti a **törzset** is (innen a *nemzetség szerint* fordítás). Ez a kettős jelentés a próba része: minden törzsnek egy *matte.*

De ami a lényeg: a bot **levágott, lefaragott, kiszárított faág.**

| Egy élő ág | Egy bot |
|---|---|
| van gyökere | **nincs** |
| vizet vesz fel | **nem** |
| növekszik | **nem** |
| virágozhat | **nem** |

Vagyis a bot pontosan az a tárgy, amelyről biztosan tudható, hogy **nem fog kivirágozni.**

És Isten éppen ezzel próbál (17:5): *Annak az embernek a botja, akit kiválasztok, **kivirágzik.***

Ez a próba lényege. A jel nem az erő, nem a többség, nem a hangosság. A jel az, hogy valami **élni kezd** ott, ahol nincs élet.

Megjegyzés: Áron botja már korábban is jel volt — a 2Mózes 7:10-12-ben a fáraó előtt kígyóvá lett. Vagyis a szöveg ugyanazzal a tárggyal dolgozik, de most nem hatalmat, hanem **életet** mutat.

**A lebonyolítás — és két részlet, amely sokat elmond**

| Vers | Mi történik | Miért fontos |
|---|---|---|
| 17:2-3 | tizenkét bot, mindegyiken a név | nem lehetett összekeverni |
| 17:6 | **Áron botja is közöttük volt** | nem kapott külön helyet |
| 17:7 | Mózes letette mindet az Úr elé | nem ember döntött |
| 17:8 | másnap: Áron botja kivirágzott | egyetlen éjszaka |
| 17:9 | Mózes kivitte, és **mindenki látta** | nyilvános jel |
| 17:10 | a botot vissza kell tenni **jelül** | megőrizhető bizonyíték |

A 17:6 félmondata (*és Áron botja is közöttük volt*) könnyen elsiklik, de fontos: a próbában **nem volt kivételezés.** Áron botja ugyanúgy egy bot volt a tizenkettő között.

És a 17:9 szerint Mózes **kivitte** mindet, és a nép *látta.* Nem bejelentés volt, hanem bemutatás.

**2. A 17:8 — három szakasz egyszerre**

*És íme, Áron botja, Lévi háza botja kivirágzott: **bimbót hajtott, virágot nyitott, és mandulát termett.***

A héber három külön kifejezést használ, és ez szándékos:

| Héber | Mit jelent | Normálisan mikor |
|---|---|---|
| *vajjácé perah* | bimbót hajtott | a virágzás előtti napok |
| *vajjácéc cíc* | virágot nyitott | tavasszal, néhány napig |
| *vajjigmól sekédím* | mandulát termett (beérett) | **hónapokkal** később |

A három szakasz a valóságban **nem lehet egyszerre** egy ágon. Amikor a gyümölcs beérik, a virág már régen lehullott.

A szöveg tehát nem egyszerűen azt mondja, hogy *kivirágzott.* Három egymást követő szakaszt **egymásra rak** — és ezzel azt jelzi, hogy ami történt, az nem egy lassú folyamat volt.

**3. A mandula — és egy szójáték Jeremiásnál**

Miért éppen mandula? Ez nem véletlen.

**Egy: a mandula az első.** A mandulafa (héberül *sákéd*) az első fa, amely kinyílik Izráel földjén: **januárban vagy februárban,** amikor minden más fa még alszik. Néha még hó is van, amikor virágzik.

**Kettő: és ebből van egy szójáték a Bibliában.**

A **Jeremiás 1:11-12**-ben ez történik:

*Mit látsz, Jeremiás? Azt mondtam: **mandulavesszőt** látok. Az Úr azt mondta: Jól láttál, mert **virrasztok** a szavam fölött, hogy beteljesítsem.*

A két szó héberül:

| Szó | Jelentés |
|---|---|
| *sákéd* | mandula |
| *sókéd* | virraszt, éber, figyel |

Szinte ugyanúgy hangzik. Vagyis a mandula a Bibliában az **éberség** és a **korai ébredés** jele: az, ami először kezd el élni.

**Három: a menóra.** A szent sátor lámpatartóját mandulavirág alakú kelyhekkel kellett megformálni (2Móz 25:33-34). Vagyis ugyanez a kép ott volt a szentélyben.

**4. A 17:10 — és egy feszültség, amelyet nem oldunk fel**

*Tedd vissza Áron botját a bizonyság **elé,** hogy megőrizzék jelül a lázadó fiaknak.* (17:10)

Figyeld meg a szót: *elé.* A héber *lifné háédút* — *a bizonyság előtt,* nem *benne.*

És most jön egy valódi feszültség a Bibliában:

| Hely | Mit mond a láda tartalmáról |
|---|---|
| 4Móz 17:10 | a bot a bizonyság **elé** került |
| Zsid 9:4 | a ládában volt *az arany füstölőoltár, a mannás korsó, **Áron botja** és a szövetség táblái* |
| 1Kir 8:9 | *a ládában **semmi más nem volt,** csak a két kőtábla* |

A három hely nem ugyanazt mondja.

Három magyarázat áll:

1. **Előtte, nem benne.** A 4Mózes 17:10 *elé* szava miatt a bot a láda **mellett** vagy **előtt** lehetett. A Zsidókhoz írt levél görög szava (*en hé*) pedig jelentheti azt is, hogy *amellyel* vagy *amelyhez tartozóan.*
2. **Más hagyomány.** A Zsidókhoz írt levél szerzője egy olyan hagyományt követ, amely a bot és a manna helyét a ládában tudta.
3. **Időközi változás.** Az 1Királyok 8:9 Salamon idejéről beszél, több száz évvel később — addig a tárgyak elkerülhettek.

**Nem tudjuk,** melyik igaz. Nem fogjuk az egyiket biztosnak mutatni, mert a három szöveghely a maga formájában nem fedi egymást.

**5. És most a legérdekesebb: a nép reakciója**

Azt gondolnánk, hogy a nép megnyugszik. A kérdés el volt döntve, a jel nyilvános volt, mindenki látta.

De ez áll a fejezet végén (17:12-13):

*Izráel fiai azt mondták Mózesnek: Íme, **elpusztulunk, elvesztünk, mindnyájan elvesztünk!** Mindenki, aki az Úr hajlékához közelít, meghal. Vajon egészen el kell pusztulnunk?*

Olvasd el újra, és figyelj arra, hogy mit **nem** mondanak. Nem azt mondják: *most már értjük.* Nem azt: *rendben van.* Nem azt: *köszönjük.*

Azt mondják: ***elpusztulunk.***

A jel megválaszolta a kérdést — és a **félelmük nem lett kevesebb, hanem több.** Most már azt látták, hogy a szentély közelsége veszélyes, és hogy ez nem tréfa.

Ez emberileg pontos megfigyelés, és érdemes kimondani: **a bizonyíték és a bizalom nem ugyanaz.** Lehet valamit tudni, és mégis félni tőle.

**6. Isten válasza — és ez a rész szíve**

A 18. fejezet első versei **pontosan erre a kiáltásra** válaszolnak. És a válasz formája a legfontosabb.

Isten **nem** azt mondja, hogy *ne félj, nincs veszély.* Nem tagadja a 17:13-at.

Ezt mondja (18:1):

*Te és a fiaid és atyád háza veled együtt **hordozzátok a szentély bűnét;** te és a fiaid hordozzátok a papságotok bűnét.*

A héber ige: *tiszú* — *hordozzátok, viseljétek.* Ugyanaz a szó, amely a 3Mózes 16:22-ben (p42) a bak esetében állt: *a bak **vigye el** magán a vétküket.*

Vagyis Isten válasza nem a veszély tagadása, hanem a **teher áthelyezése.**

És a 18:5 megadja a célt: *hogy **ne legyen többé harag** Izráel fiain.*

Most tedd egymás mellé a két mondatot:

| A nép kérdése (17:13) | A válasz (18:1, 5) |
|---|---|
| *mindenki, aki közelít, meghal* | a papok hordozzák a szentély bűnét |
| *egészen el kell pusztulnunk?* | hogy ne legyen többé harag a népen |

Vagyis a papság ebben a fejezetben nem **kiváltság,** hanem **védelem** — a nép védelme, a papok terhére.

És ez pontosan az, ami a p51 Kórah-kérdését a másik oldaláról világítja meg. Kórah azt kérdezte: *miért nem lehet az enyém is?* A 18. fejezet pedig megmutatja, **mi az,** amit kért.

**7. A 18:7 — a szó, amely mindent eldönt**

*Te pedig és a fiaid veled együtt végezzétek a papságot mindabban, ami az oltárhoz és a függöny mögé tartozik. **Ajándékul adtam nektek a papságotokat.***

A héber szó: *mattáná* — **ajándék.**

És most vesd össze a két mondatot:

| Kórah (4Móz 16:10) | A válasz (4Móz 18:7) |
|---|---|
| *és most a papságot is **keresitek?*** | *ajándékul **adtam** nektek a papságotokat* |
| a héber ige: *bikkés* (keres, igyekszik megszerezni) | a héber szó: *mattáná* (ajándék) |

A válasz tehát nem egyszerűen az, hogy *Áron az, és nem te.* A válasz az, hogy a papság **olyan fajta dolog,** amelyet nem lehet megszerezni — csak kapni.

És ehhez még egy részlet: a **18:6** szerint a **léviták** is *ajándékul adattak* a papoknak. Vagyis mind a két szolgálat ajándék volt:

| Ki | Mit kapott | Honnan |
|---|---|---|
| Áron és fiai | a papságot | *ajándékul adtam nektek* (18:7) |
| Áron és fiai | a lévitákat a szolgálathoz | *ajándékul adattak nektek* (18:6) |
| a léviták | a sátor szolgálatát | kiválasztás (16:9) |

Senki nem érdemelte ki a magáét.

**8. Mit mond erről az Újszövetség?**

A **Zsidókhoz írt levél 5:4** pontosan ezt a gondolatot veszi fel:

*Senki nem veszi magának ezt a tisztességet, hanem akit Isten hív el, mint Áront is.*

És a következő versben Jézusra alkalmazza ugyanezt: ő sem *magának vette* a főpapságot.

Vagyis az Újszövetség ugyanazt a pontot emeli ki, amelyet a 4Mózes 18:7: ez olyan dolog, amelyet **adnak.**

**Mi lesz a következő részben?**

A p53-ban jön a 4Mózes 20: **víz a sziklából.** Ez a könyv egyik legszomorúbb fejezete, mert három dolog van benne:

| Vers | Mi történik |
|---|---|
| 20:1 | meghal **Mirjám** — egyetlen rövid mondatban, gyászleírás nélkül |
| 20:10-12 | **Mózes hibázik** a szikla előtt, és nem mehet be a földre |
| 20:28 | meghal **Áron** a hegyen |

És ott lesz az a kérdés, amelyet nem lehet kihagyni, és amelyre a szöveg nem ad egyértelmű választ: **mit tett Mózes olyan rosszul?**

o: A proba targya tizenket BOT volt - levagott, holt faagak
A bot eppen az, ami nem tud kivirágozni: nincs gyokere es nincs eletje
A 17:8 szerint az egyiken bimbo, virag ES beért mandula volt egyszerre
Vagyis a valasz nem szavazas vagy erő volt, hanem hogy valami ELNI kezdett
oe: The subject of the test was twelve STAFFS - cut, dead branches
A staff is precisely what cannot bud: it has no root and no life
By 17:8 one of them had buds, blossoms AND ripe almonds at once
So the answer was not a vote or strength but that something began to LIVE

v.t: Másnap Mózes bement a bizonyság sátorába, és íme, Áron botja, Lévi háza botja kivirágzott: bimbót hajtott, virágot nyitott, és mandulát termett.

o: A 4Moz 17:10 azt mondja: tedd vissza a botot a bizonyság ELE
A Zsid 9:4 szerint a ladaban volt a ket ko, a manna es Aron botja
De az 1Kir 8:9 szerint a ladaban SEMMI MAS nem volt, csak a ket ko
Harom magyarazat all (elotte vagy benne; mas hagyomany; idokozi valtozas), es nem tudjuk
oe: Num 17:10 says: put the staff back BEFORE the testimony
By Heb 9:4 the ark held the two tablets, the manna and the staff of Aaron
But by 1 Kgs 8:9 there was NOTHING ELSE in the ark but the two tablets
Three explanations stand (before or inside; a different tradition; change over time), and we do not know

v.t: Az Úr azt mondta Mózesnek: Tedd vissza Áron botját a bizonyság elé, hogy megőrizzék jelül a lázadó fiaknak, hogy megszűnjön a zúgolódásuk előlem, és ne haljanak meg.

o: A nep a jel utan NEM megnyugodott: mindenki, aki kozelit, meghal (17:13)
Isten valasza nem az, hogy nincs veszely
Hanem az, hogy a PAPOK hordozzak a szentély bunét (18:1)
Es a 18:7 szerint maga a papsag AJANDEK (mattana) - nem megszerezhető
oe: After the sign the people were NOT relieved: everyone who comes near dies (17:13)
The answer of God is not that there is no danger
But that the PRIESTS bear the guilt of the sanctuary (18:1)
And by 18:7 the priesthood itself is a GIFT (mattanah) - it cannot be seized

v.t: Te pedig és a fiaid veled együtt végezzétek a papságot mindabban, ami az oltárhoz és a függöny mögé tartozik. Ajándékul adtam nektek a papságotokat.

story.e:
**Twelve Dead Branches — and the Next Morning One of Them Has Almonds**

In p51 Korah asked a question: who may bring incense before God? Who may be a priest?

And now comes the answer. But not the way you would expect.

**Not a Vote. Not a Trial of Strength. Not an Argument.**

This is how the test ran (17:2):

*Take from them a staff for each clan, from every leader of their fathers house, **twelve staffs;** write the name of each on his staff.*

Twelve **staffs.** Each with the name of its owner written on it.

And now notice something important.

**What Is a Staff?**

A staff is a **cut branch.** Someone once cut it from a tree, shaped it, and has used it since — leaning on it, driving the flock with it.

So a staff is **dead wood.** It has no root, no leaves, it does not grow, and it does not blossom.

And that is the point of the test.

**What Did God Say?**

*The staff of the man whom I choose will **bud.*** (17:5)

He did not say: whoever is strongest. Not: whoever is cleverest. Not: whoever gets the most votes.

He said: the staff that **begins to live.**

**What Happened?**

Moses laid all twelve staffs in the tent, before God (17:7). The staff of Aaron was **among the others** (17:6) — it got no special place.

And the next day (17:8):

*The next day Moses went into the tent of the testimony, and behold, **the staff of Aaron** had budded: **it put out buds, opened blossoms and bore almonds.***

Read the end again and count how many things are in it:

1. **it put out buds**
2. **it opened blossoms**
3. **it bore almonds**

Three stages — and **all three at once** on the staff.

In reality this would take months: first buds, then blossoms, then — much later — the ripe fruit. Here all three are there at once.

**Why Almonds?**

This is a lovely detail. The **almond tree** is the first tree to blossom in that land — in January or February, when everything else is still asleep.

So the almond is the sign of the **earliest waking.**

**And What Happened Afterwards?**

*Moses brought all the staffs out from before the LORD to all the Israelites; and **they looked,** and each took his own staff.* (17:9)

Everyone saw it. It was not a secret sign.

And God said that the staff of Aaron should be **put back** before the testimony, *to be kept as a **sign*** (17:10). So that it could be looked at later too.

**And Now Something You Would Not Expect**

You would think the people were relieved. After all, the answer was there.

But that is not what happened (17:12-13):

*The Israelites said to Moses: Behold, **we perish, we are lost, we are all lost!** Everyone who comes near the tabernacle of the LORD dies. Must we be utterly destroyed?*

So they were not relieved. They were **terrified.**

The question was settled — and they were more afraid than before.

**And What Did God Answer to That?**

This is the most interesting part of all.

God did **not** say *do not be afraid, there is nothing wrong.* He said this (18:1):

*You and your sons and the house of your father with you are to **bear the guilt of the sanctuary;** you and your sons are to bear the guilt of your priesthood.*

That is: the fear is justified — but it is not for you to carry. **The priests carry it.**

And 18:5 says why: *so that there may be **no more anger** on the Israelites.*

So the priestly service was not there to make someone important. It was there so the people would be **safe.**

**And the Loveliest Sentence**

*And you and your sons with you are to carry out the priesthood... **I have given you your priesthood as a gift.*** (18:7)

**As a gift.**

Now think through what the question of Korah was: *why can it not be mine too?*

And the answer: because this is not a thing that can be **obtained.** It is a thing that is **given.**

**What Comes Next?**

In p53 comes Numbers 20: **water from the rock** — and this will be the day when Moses makes a mistake. And in that chapter Miriam and Aaron both die.

It is one of the saddest chapters in Numbers.
story.m:
**Twelve Dead Branches — and the Next Morning One of Them Has Almonds**

In p51 Korah asked a question: **who may be a priest?** Who may bring incense before God?

And now comes the answer. But the manner of the answer is the most interesting thing in it.

**What the Test Was NOT**

It is worth first seeing what God did **not** do:

| What he did not do | Although he could have |
|---|---|
| he did not put it to a vote of the people | since by 16:3 the whole people is holy |
| he did not arrange a trial of strength | since the test of censers had already happened (16:16-18) |
| he did not argue | since Moses had already argued (16:9-11) |
| he did not leave the decision to Moses | although he was the leader |

Instead he commanded this (17:2):

*Take from them a staff for each clan... **twelve staffs;** write the name of each on his staff.*

**What Is a Staff?**

This is worth pausing on, because it is the key to the test.

A staff is a **cut branch.** Shaped, dried wood. It has no root, no leaves, it takes up no water, and it does not grow.

So a staff is precisely the thing that **cannot bud.**

And God tests with exactly that (17:5):

*The staff of the man whom I choose will **bud;** so I will silence before me the complaining of the Israelites.*

Notice what the sign is: not strength, not numbers, not argument. But that something **begins to live** where there can be no life.

**The Procedure — and One Important Detail**

| Verse | What happens |
|---|---|
| 17:2-3 | twelve staffs, each with the name of the leader; the name of Aaron on the staff of Levi |
| 17:6 | each leader gives a staff — and **the staff of Aaron is among them** |
| 17:7 | Moses lays them all before the LORD |
| 17:8 | **the next day** the staff of Aaron had budded |
| 17:9 | Moses brought them all out, and **everyone saw** |
| 17:10 | the staff of Aaron is to be put back, as a **sign** |

Two details are worth remembering.

**The first:** by 17:6 *the staff of Aaron was **among** them.* So it got no special place. It was laid down like the rest.

**The second:** by 17:9 Moses **brought out** the staffs, and the people *looked.* The sign was public — Moses did not announce it; everyone saw with their own eyes.

**17:8 — Three Stages at Once**

*And behold, the staff of Aaron, the staff of the house of Levi, had budded: **it put out buds, opened blossoms and bore almonds.***

Count how many things are in this half-sentence:

| Stage | Normally when |
|---|---|
| buds | the days before blossoming |
| blossoms | in spring, for a few days |
| ripe almonds | **months** later |

In reality the three stages cannot occur **at once** on one branch. The text piles them up deliberately.

**Why Almonds?**

This is not an accidental choice, and it is worth knowing why.

The **almond tree** is the first tree to blossom in that land: in **January or February,** when every other tree is still asleep. In Hebrew *shaqed.*

And from this comes a wordplay in the Bible. In **Jeremiah 1:11-12** God shows the prophet an **almond branch** and says: *you have seen rightly, for I am **watching** over my word to fulfil it.* The word for *watching* in Hebrew is *shoqed* — it sounds almost the same as *shaqed* (almond).

So in the Bible the almond is the sign of **wakefulness** and **early waking.**

And one more thing: the **menorah,** the lampstand of the holy tent, was decorated with cups shaped like almond blossoms (Ex 25:33-34).

**And Now Something You Would Not Expect**

You would think the people are relieved. The answer is there, the sign was public, everyone saw it.

But this happened (17:12-13):

*The Israelites said to Moses: Behold, **we perish, we are lost, we are all lost!** Everyone who comes near the tabernacle of the LORD dies. Must we be utterly destroyed?*

So they were **not relieved. They were terrified.**

The question was settled — and their fear did not become less but greater. Now they saw that the nearness of the sanctuary is **dangerous.**

This is a humanly accurate observation: proof and trust are not the same.

**And the Answer of God — the Most Interesting Part**

The first verses of chapter 18 answer **exactly this question.** And look at how.

God does **not** say *do not be afraid, there is no danger.* He says this (18:1):

*You and your sons and the house of your father with you are to **bear the guilt of the sanctuary;** you and your sons are to bear the guilt of your priesthood.*

That is: the fear is **not groundless** — but someone bears the burden. And it is not the people.

And 18:5 gives the aim: *so that there may be **no more anger** on the Israelites.*

That is the meaning of the whole priestly service in this chapter. Not the rank. Not the privilege. **The burden.**

**And Now the Loveliest Sentence**

*And you and your sons with you are to carry out the priesthood in everything belonging to the altar and behind the curtain. **I have given you your priesthood as a gift.*** (18:7)

The Hebrew word for *gift* is *mattanah.*

And now compare this with the request of Korah:

| Korah (16:10) | The answer (18:7) |
|---|---|
| *you are seeking the priesthood as well* | *I have given it to you as a gift* |
| he wanted to obtain it | a thing that can only be **given** |

So the answer is not that Korah was bad and Aaron good. The answer is that **this is not a thing that can be obtained.**

And it is worth noting: by 18:6 the **Levites** too were *given as a gift* to the priests. So both were gifts. No one earned anything.

**What Comes Next?**

In p53 comes Numbers 20: **water from the rock.**

It is one of the saddest chapters in Numbers. Three things happen in it:

- **Miriam** dies (20:1), in a single short sentence
- **Moses makes a mistake** before the rock (20:10-12)
- and **Aaron** dies (20:28)

And there stands the question that cannot be left out: what did Moses do so badly that he could not enter the land?
story.h:
**Twelve Dead Branches — and the Next Morning One of Them Has Almonds**

In p51 Korah asked a question, and the question was a good one: **who may be a priest?** Who may bring incense before God?

This part contains the answer. And the manner of the answer is the most interesting thing in it.

We have four things to deal with:

1. the **nature** of the test — and why with a staff
2. the **three stages** of 17:8 at once
3. the almond, and a wordplay in Jeremiah
4. and most importantly: that the reaction of the people was **not** relief — and what God answered to it

**A Note About the Numbering**

Before we begin, a practical matter that can be confusing.

In the **Hebrew** Bible these verses carry the numbers **17:16-28.** This is because the Hebrew text begins chapter 17 where most English and Hungarian Bibles place the end of chapter 16 (the plates from the censers and the plague).

That is:

| What | English numbering | Hebrew numbering |
|---|---|---|
| the plates from the censers | 16:36-40 | 17:1-5 |
| the plague and the running of Aaron | 16:41-50 | 17:6-15 |
| **the twelve staffs** | **17:1-13** | **17:16-28** |

We follow the numbering customary in Hungarian Bibles, as in the rest of the game. But anyone looking in another Bible may find different numbers. This is not an error but two traditions.

**1. The Nature of the Test — and Why with a Staff**

First it is worth seeing what God did **not** do:

| What he did not do | Although it would have been logical |
|---|---|
| he did not hold a vote | by 16:3 the whole people is holy — asking them would have been obvious |
| he did not arrange a trial of strength | the test of censers was such a thing (16:16-18) |
| he did not argue further | Moses had already argued (16:9-11) |
| Moses did not decide | although he was the leader |

Instead he commanded this (17:2):

*Take from them a staff for each clan, from every leader of their fathers house, **twelve staffs;** write the name of each on his staff.*

**Now think through what a staff is.**

The Hebrew word: *matteh.* It means staff, rod, branch — and the same word also means **tribe** (hence the rendering *for each clan*). This double meaning is part of the test: one *matteh* for each tribe.

But the point is this: a staff is a **cut, shaped, dried branch.**

| A living branch | A staff |
|---|---|
| has a root | **does not** |
| takes up water | **does not** |
| grows | **does not** |
| can blossom | **cannot** |

So a staff is precisely the object about which it is certain that it **will not bud.**

And God tests with exactly that (17:5): *the staff of the man whom I choose will **bud.***

That is the point of the test. The sign is not strength, not a majority, not loudness. The sign is that something **begins to live** where there is no life.

A note: the staff of Aaron had already been a sign before — in Exodus 7:10-12 it became a serpent before Pharaoh. So the text works with the same object, but now it shows not power but **life.**

**The Procedure — and Two Details That Say Much**

| Verse | What happens | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| 17:2-3 | twelve staffs, each with the name | they could not be confused |
| 17:6 | **the staff of Aaron was among them** | it got no special place |
| 17:7 | Moses laid them all before the LORD | no person decided |
| 17:8 | the next day: the staff of Aaron had budded | a single night |
| 17:9 | Moses brought them out, and **everyone saw** | a public sign |
| 17:10 | the staff is to be put back as a **sign** | storable evidence |

The half-sentence of 17:6 (*and the staff of Aaron was among them*) is easily missed, but it matters: in the test there was **no favouritism.** The staff of Aaron was one staff among the twelve.

And by 17:9 Moses **brought** them all out, and the people *looked.* It was not an announcement but a showing.

**2. 17:8 — Three Stages at Once**

*And behold, the staff of Aaron, the staff of the house of Levi, had budded: **it put out buds, opened blossoms and bore almonds.***

The Hebrew uses three separate expressions, and this is deliberate:

| Hebrew | What it means | Normally when |
|---|---|---|
| *wayyotse perah* | it put out buds | the days before blossoming |
| *wayyatsets tsits* | it opened blossoms | in spring, for a few days |
| *wayyigmol sheqedim* | it bore (ripened) almonds | **months** later |

In reality the three stages **cannot be at once** on one branch. By the time the fruit ripens, the blossom has long fallen.

So the text does not simply say that it *budded.* It **stacks** three consecutive stages on top of each other — and in so doing signals that what happened was not a slow process.

**3. The Almond — and a Wordplay in Jeremiah**

Why almonds? This is not accidental.

**One: the almond is first.** The almond tree (in Hebrew *shaqed*) is the first tree to blossom in the land of Israel: in **January or February,** when every other tree is still asleep. Sometimes there is still snow when it blossoms.

**Two: and from this comes a wordplay in the Bible.**

In **Jeremiah 1:11-12** this happens:

*What do you see, Jeremiah? I said: I see an **almond branch.** The LORD said: You have seen rightly, for I am **watching** over my word to fulfil it.*

The two words in Hebrew:

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| *shaqed* | almond |
| *shoqed* | watching, awake, attentive |

They sound almost the same. So in the Bible the almond is the sign of **wakefulness** and **early waking:** the thing that begins to live first.

**Three: the menorah.** The lampstand of the holy tent was to be shaped with cups like almond blossoms (Ex 25:33-34). So the same image was there in the sanctuary.

**4. 17:10 — and a Tension We Do Not Resolve**

*Put the staff of Aaron back **before** the testimony, to be kept as a sign for the rebellious sons.* (17:10)

Notice the word: *before.* The Hebrew *lifnei haedut* — *before the testimony,* not *in* it.

And now comes a real tension in the Bible:

| Place | What it says about the contents of the ark |
|---|---|
| Num 17:10 | the staff was placed **before** the testimony |
| Heb 9:4 | in the ark were *the golden altar of incense, the jar of manna, **the staff of Aaron** and the tablets of the covenant* |
| 1 Kgs 8:9 | *there was **nothing else** in the ark but the two tablets* |

The three passages do not say the same thing.

Three explanations stand:

1. **Before, not inside.** Because of the word *before* in Numbers 17:10, the staff may have been **beside** or **in front of** the ark. And the Greek phrase in Hebrews (*en he*) can also mean *with which* or *belonging to which.*
2. **A different tradition.** The author of Hebrews follows a tradition that located the staff and the manna inside the ark.
3. **Change over time.** 1 Kings 8:9 speaks of the time of Solomon, several centuries later — by then the objects may have been removed.

**We do not know** which is true. We will not present one as certain, because the three passages in their own form do not cover one another.

**5. And Now the Most Interesting Part: the Reaction of the People**

We would think the people are relieved. The question was settled, the sign was public, everyone saw it.

But this stands at the end of the chapter (17:12-13):

*The Israelites said to Moses: Behold, **we perish, we are lost, we are all lost!** Everyone who comes near the tabernacle of the LORD dies. Must we be utterly destroyed?*

Read it again and notice what they do **not** say. They do not say: *now we understand.* Not: *that is all right.* Not: *thank you.*

They say: ***we perish.***

The sign answered the question — and their **fear became greater, not less.** Now they saw that the nearness of the sanctuary is dangerous, and that this is no joke.

This is a humanly accurate observation, and it is worth saying: **proof and trust are not the same.** One can know something and still fear it.

**6. The Answer of God — and This Is the Heart of the Part**

The first verses of chapter 18 answer **exactly this cry.** And the form of the answer matters most.

God does **not** say *do not be afraid, there is no danger.* He does not deny 17:13.

He says this (18:1):

*You and your sons and the house of your father with you are to **bear the guilt of the sanctuary;** you and your sons are to bear the guilt of your priesthood.*

The Hebrew verb: *tisu* — *bear, carry.* The same word that stood in Leviticus 16:22 (p42) for the goat: *the goat is to **carry away** their offences on itself.*

So the answer of God is not a denial of the danger but a **transfer of the burden.**

And 18:5 gives the aim: *so that there may be **no more anger** on the Israelites.*

Now set the two sentences side by side:

| The question of the people (17:13) | The answer (18:1, 5) |
|---|---|
| *everyone who comes near dies* | the priests bear the guilt of the sanctuary |
| *must we be utterly destroyed?* | so that there may be no more anger on the people |

So in this chapter the priesthood is not a **privilege** but a **protection** — the protection of the people, at the cost of the priests.

And this is exactly what lights up the Korah question of p51 from the other side. Korah asked: *why can it not be mine too?* And chapter 18 shows **what** it was that he asked for.

**7. 18:7 — the Word That Settles Everything**

*And you and your sons with you are to carry out the priesthood in everything belonging to the altar and behind the curtain. **I have given you your priesthood as a gift.***

The Hebrew word: *mattanah* — **gift.**

And now compare the two sentences:

| Korah (Num 16:10) | The answer (Num 18:7) |
|---|---|
| *and now you are **seeking** the priesthood as well?* | *I have **given** you your priesthood as a gift* |
| the Hebrew verb: *biqqesh* (to seek, to try to obtain) | the Hebrew word: *mattanah* (gift) |

So the answer is not simply that *Aaron is the one and you are not.* The answer is that the priesthood is **the kind of thing** that cannot be obtained — only received.

And one more detail: by **18:6** the **Levites** too were *given as a gift* to the priests. So both services were gifts:

| Who | What they received | From where |
|---|---|---|
| Aaron and his sons | the priesthood | *I have given it to you as a gift* (18:7) |
| Aaron and his sons | the Levites for the service | *they are given to you as a gift* (18:6) |
| the Levites | the service of the tent | by choosing (16:9) |

No one earned their own.

**8. What Does the New Testament Say About This?**

**Hebrews 5:4** takes up exactly this thought:

*No one takes this honour for himself, but he is called by God, just as Aaron was.*

And in the next verse it applies the same to Jesus: he too did not *take for himself* the high priesthood.

So the New Testament highlights the same point as Numbers 18:7: this is a thing that is **given.**

**What Comes Next?**

In p53 comes Numbers 20: **water from the rock.** It is one of the saddest chapters in the book, because three things are in it:

| Verse | What happens |
|---|---|
| 20:1 | **Miriam** dies — in a single short sentence, with no account of mourning |
| 20:10-12 | **Moses makes a mistake** before the rock, and may not enter the land |
| 20:28 | **Aaron** dies on the mountain |

And there stands the question that cannot be left out, and to which the text gives no unambiguous answer: **what did Moses do so badly?**
