story.e:
This is a story about five young women who did something nobody had done before.

There was a man named **Zelophehad.** He died in the wilderness, like his whole generation. He left no son behind - only five daughters: **Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah.**

In those days land passed from father to son. Without a son, a family's name simply disappeared from the lists, and the land went to someone else. Everyone knew this, and nobody thought it could be changed.

The five daughters went anyway.

Look at **where** they went, because this is the most surprising part of the story: *they stood before Moses, before Eleazar the priest, before the leaders and before the whole community at the entrance of the tent of meeting* (27:2). They did not send a male relative in their place. They did not ask someone quietly. They stood in the most public place that camp had.

And they laid out their case. In three sentences (27:3-4). Precisely, calmly, and ending with a question that had no ready answer: *why should our father's name disappear from his clan because he had no son?*

Now comes the reason this story is worth remembering.

**Moses did not answer.**

He was the lawgiver. He brought the commands down from the mountain. And now five young women asked him a question, and he did not know the answer. Verse 27:5 says it very simply: *and Moses brought their case before the LORD.*

He did not make something up. He did not say *it has always been this way.* He asked.

And the answer came: ***the daughters of Zelophehad are right.*** (27:7)

Read that again. God said the daughters were **right** - in a matter about the law. And it did not stop there. In 27:8 a new rule is made for all Israel: if a man dies and has no son, his daughter inherits his land.

Five young women asked, and the law changed.

**The other half of the chapter**, which many people forget: in this same chapter Moses learns that he himself will not enter that land. He may go up a mountain and look at it - but he will not set foot on it.

And notice what he says in reply. He does not talk about himself. He asks that there be someone to lead the people, *so that the community of the LORD will not be like a flock without a shepherd* (27:17). That sentence became very well known later - Jesus said it too, when he looked at the crowds (Matthew 9:36).

And so **Joshua** became the next leader.

**And now the harder half of the story.** Much later, in the last chapter of Numbers, the relatives of these women - the male clan heads - come back and raise a problem: if these daughters choose husbands from elsewhere, the land they were given will move to another tribe.

The ruling: they may marry *whoever seems good to them* - but within their father's tribe (36:6). And so it was: they married the sons of their uncles (36:11).

We will talk more about this second half on the medium and hard levels, because it is not simple, and there are two ways of seeing it.

But one thing is certainly true: **the book of Numbers ends here.** Not with entering the land. With an inheritance case brought by five women, on the bank of the Jordan, opposite Jericho. The book itself chose to put this at the very end.
story.m:
Numbers 27 sets two stories side by side that seem to have nothing to do with each other: the inheritance case of five women, and the news of the death of Moses. Let us look at both, and then at what returns at the end of the book, in chapter 36.

**1. Who stood there**

Verse 27:1 does not shorten the list. It gives the full descent - Zelophehad, Hepher, Gilead, Machir, Manasseh - and writes out all five names: **Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah.** This is not accidental. In a book full of lists of men, this sentence names five women and gives their whole family line as well.

**2. Where they stood**

Verse 27:2 is very precise: *before Moses, before Eleazar the priest, before the leaders and before the whole community at the entrance of the tent of meeting.* Those four levels together are the entire leadership of the camp, in the open. The case was not handled in whispers, nor through a male relative. They took it to the most public place there was.

**3. What they said - and how shrewdly**

Their argument has three steps (27:3-4):

First they **distance themselves**: *he was not among those who gathered with Korah against the LORD.* Nobody asked them this. They say it themselves, because the rebellion of Korah (which we looked at in p51) was still fresh in memory, and a request from the family of a rebel would have sounded very different.

Second they **state the fact**: their father *died for his own sin.* This phrase most likely does not point to some particular crime, but to the judgement that fell on the whole wilderness generation (Num 14). For the text **never says what Zelophehad did.** More on this on the hard level.

Third they **ask the question**: *why should our father's name disappear?* Notice how they word it. They do not say *it is owed to us.* They say their **father's name** will vanish. Whether this was sincere conviction or clever argument we cannot know - and it was probably both.

**4. Moses does not know the answer**

Verse 27:5 is five words in the original, and yet it is the spine of the chapter: *and Moses brought their case before the LORD.*

The lawgiver says: **I do not know.** He does not improvise, and he does not appeal to the way things have always been.

And this is not a one-off. Four times in the Torah a case comes to Moses that he cannot decide, and he takes it up: the case of the blasphemer (Lev 24:12), of those who could not keep the Passover because of uncleanness (Num 9:8), of the man gathering wood on the Sabbath (Num 15:34), and this one. In two of the four the case ends with **a new rule being made.**

**5. The answer**

*The daughters of Zelophehad are right* (27:7). Their case wins itself, and 27:8 turns it into general law: in the absence of a son, the daughter inherits.

Here we must be precise, because a lot of overstatement circulates about this. The ruling did **not** make daughters equal heirs with sons: they inherit when there is no son. But neither is it true that nothing happened - the law changed, and it changed because five people asked.

**6. The other half of the chapter**

In 27:12 Moses learns: he may go up Mount Abarim and look at the land, but he will not set foot on it.

And now comes the thing that links the two stories. The reply of Moses is not about himself. He asks (27:16-17) that the LORD appoint someone over the people, *so that the community of the LORD will not be like a flock without a shepherd.* A man who has just learned he will not reach the goal speaks about what will become of everyone else.

This image became famous later: Jesus looked over the crowds with these same words (Matthew 9:36; Mark 6:34).

Joshua becomes the leader (27:18-23). But watch the details, because the text quietly makes a distinction here: Moses is to give him *of his authority* (27:20) - that is, a share, not all of it - and Joshua must enquire through Eleazar the priest (27:21), whereas God spoke with Moses directly (Num 12:8). Joshua is not a second Moses, and the text does not claim he is.

**7. And the end of the book: chapter 36**

In the very last chapter of Numbers the case returns - but now from the side of the male clan heads (36:1-3). Their argument is sensible: if the daughters choose husbands from another tribe, their land goes on with that tribe, and the inheritance of Manasseh is reduced.

The ruling (36:6): they may marry *whoever seems good to them* - but within their father's tribe. And according to 36:10-11 that is what they did: they married the sons of their uncles.

This chapter must not be passed over in silence, and it must not be simplified either. There are two ways of seeing it, and both have a basis in the text - we will go through this in detail on the hard level.

One thing is worth seeing already: **the book of Numbers ends here** (36:13). Not with the conquest of the land. With the inheritance case of five women, on the plains of Moab, by the Jordan, opposite Jericho.
story.h:
Numbers 27 and 36, read together, make up one of the most interesting legal narratives in the Bible: a request that changes the law, and a counter-request that partly pulls it back. Let us go through it carefully - and say also what the text does not say.

**1. The list that is not shortened**

Verse 27:1 names five women: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, Tirzah - and gives the full descent back to Manasseh. This happens in a book that begins and ends with two great censuses, in which men are counted.

Worth noticing: these five names return three more times in the Bible (Num 26:33; 36:11; Josh 17:3), and besides these 1 Chronicles 7:15 mentions Zelophehad as well. An inheritance case rarely gets this much room.

**2. Publicity as a tool**

Verse 27:2 lists four addressees: Moses, Eleazar the priest, the leaders, and **the whole community** - at the entrance of the tent of meeting. That is the most public point in the camp.

This is strategy. A private request can be brushed aside; this one cannot. The text does not judge whether it was courage or calculation - it only records where they stood.

**3. The three layers of the argument**

**(a) The distancing.** *He was not among those who gathered with Korah against the LORD* (27:3). Nobody asked this. They raise it themselves.

Why? Because after the rebellion of Korah (Num 16) a land claim from the family of a rebel would have been hopeless. The five women take the strongest counter-argument off the table in advance. That is legal instinct.

**(b) The fact the text does not unfold.** *He died for his own sin* (27:3). What did Zelophehad do?

**The text never says.** The most likely reading is that this does not point to a particular crime but to the judgement of Numbers 14: the whole generation that came out of Egypt died in the wilderness. The daughters are saying: our father was no better and no worse than the rest.

There is another tradition that identifies Zelophehad with the man gathering wood on the Sabbath (Num 15:32-36). But that is **pure inference**, not a claim of the text - the Bible nowhere connects the two. We mention it as a possibility, not as a fact.

**(c) The question.** *Why should our father's name disappear?* (27:4) The request is built on their father's name, not on their own rights.

Whether this was conviction or skilful framing we cannot know. Both are honourable, and the two do not exclude each other. Anyone claiming it was *merely* tactics says more than the text does; so does anyone claiming their own situation did not concern them.

**4. The lawgiver who does not know**

*And Moses brought their case before the LORD* (27:5).

This sentence says more about Moses than many longer passages. There is a new situation for which there is no rule, and he does not improvise.

There are four such places in the Torah, and it is worth seeing them together:
- the case of the blasphemer (Lev 24:10-23),
- those who could not keep the Passover because of uncleanness (Num 9:6-14),
- the man gathering wood on the Sabbath (Num 15:32-36),
- and this one (Num 27:1-11).

In two of them - the Passover and this - the case ends with **new legislation** that nobody had asked for. According to Numbers, then, the law did not arrive in a single block: it also grew in answer to questions.

**5. *They are right* - and what must not be concluded from it**

Verse 27:7 is very short in Hebrew: the daughters *speak rightly.* Then 27:8-11 turns it into a general order of succession: in the absence of a son the daughter, then the brothers, then the paternal uncles, then the nearest relative.

Two overstatements have to be guarded against here.

The first: that this created **equal inheritance.** It did not. A daughter inherits when there is no son. The order remains.

The second: that **nothing substantial happened.** That is not true either. The law changed, it was written down, and it was later actually applied: Joshua 17:3-6 records that the daughters of Zelophehad **did receive** land within the territory of Manasseh. It was not a victory in principle; it was carried out.

**6. The other half of the chapter - and why the two are together**

In 27:12-14 Moses learns that he will not go in. The mountain is named Abarim; Deuteronomy 34 later specifies it as Nebo.

His reply (27:15-17) is not about himself. He asks for a successor, *so that the community of the LORD will not be like a flock without a shepherd.*

The image neither begins nor ends here: it appears in 1 Kings 22:17 and in Ezekiel 34, and in the Gospels Jesus looks over the crowds with the same sentence (Matt 9:36; Mark 6:34). The connection here is real: the same expression, the same meaning.

**Why are the two stories in one chapter?** The text does not say. But one thing can be observed without reading anything in: both are about **what will become of those who come after us.** Five women stand up for their father's name; Moses asks for the future leadership of the people. Whether the editor placed them side by side for that reason, we do not know.

**7. Joshua - and what the text quietly does not give him**

Verses 27:18-23 are the installation of Joshua. Two details matter, and both are easy to skim past:

Verse 27:20: *give him of your authority.* The Hebrew word means a **share**, not the whole. Joshua does not receive everything that belonged to Moses.

Verse 27:21: Joshua must stand before Eleazar the priest, who enquires of the decision of the LORD for him by the Urim. Compare this with Numbers 12:8, where God says of Moses: *I speak with him face to face.* The directness is gone.

The text nowhere comments on this. It does not say Joshua is less. It simply describes his access differently. That is worth noticing, and worth not overstating.

**8. Chapter 36 - the hard part we do not leave out**

In the last chapter of Numbers the clan heads of Gilead - that is, the male leaders of the daughters' own tribe - come back (36:1-4). Their argument is precise and not malicious: if the daughters marry into another tribe, the land goes on with that tribe, and not even the jubilee year restores it.

The ruling (36:6): *let them marry whoever seems good to them, but only within the clan of their father's tribe.* And according to 36:10-11 that is what they did: they married the sons of their uncles.

Two readings stand, and **both have a basis**:

**The first:** this addition **protects** the result of chapter 27. The ruling would be pointless if the land slipped out of the family in the next generation. The restriction ensures that the daughters and their children actually keep what they were given.

**The second:** this addition **narrows.** In chapter 27 the request of the daughters contained no condition, and neither did the answer. Chapter 36 adds a condition afterwards that limits their freedom to marry - and the initiative came not from them but from their male relatives.

Both readings are honest. The text does not decide between them, and neither do we. What is not allowed: acting as if chapter 36 were not there, or as if it added nothing.

One thing the text itself highlights: by 36:6 the choice is **theirs** - *whoever seems good to them* - only the circle is narrower. This is not being married off; it is a framed choice. That is what it says, and no more.

**9. Marriage within the family - so that it is not misread**

According to 36:11 they married the sons of their uncles, that is, their cousins.

In that period and that society this was ordinary, and here it was expressly about keeping land and family together. The text **describes** what happened - it is not giving us advice about whom to marry today. The Bible describes many customs in many places that it does not prescribe.

**10. The list that changes**

A small but checkable detail. The order in 27:1 is: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, Tirzah. The order in 36:11 is: Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, Noah.

The order is different, and **the text does not say why.** People often suggest age, or the order of the marriages, but that is guesswork. We do not know. It is worth noticing such things, and worth not inventing an explanation for them.

**11. How the book ends**

Verse 36:13 closes Numbers: *these are the commands and decisions that the LORD gave through Moses to the Israelites on the plains of Moab, by the Jordan, opposite Jericho.*

The book that began at Sinai and travelled forty years ends neither with the conquest of the land nor with the death of Moses - that comes at the end of Deuteronomy. It ends **at the border**, with an inheritance case brought in by five women.

What can be honestly learned from this? At least this much: in Numbers most requests were complaints - for meat, for water, to go back to Egypt. These five people also asked for something, and theirs is the only request in the book of which God says: **they are right.** The difference was not that they were louder. The difference was what they asked, and how.

bio.hu: A szent sátor fő művese. Isten a Lelkével töltötte be, bölcsességgel és kézügyességgel, hogy arannyal, ezüsttel, rézzel, kővel és fával dolgozzon. Ő a Biblia első embere, akiről azt olvassuk, hogy Isten Lelke betöltötte — és nem prófétálni, hanem alkotni.
bio.en: The chief craftsman of the tabernacle. God filled him with his Spirit, with skill and ability to work in gold, silver, bronze, stone and wood. He is the first person in the Bible said to be filled with God's Spirit — and that was for making things, not for prophesying.
